title: China's AI boom to drive data centre power demand to 774 TWh by 2030
gist: Wood Mackenzie forecasts China's data centre electricity use quadrupling to 774 TWh by 2030 (6% of national power, 17% by 2060), with eight national hubs holding over 70% of capacity and emissions peaking by 2035. The core shift is from 'power follows compute' to 'compute follows power', with latency-tolerant AI training migrating to renewable-rich western China while commercial, security and CAPEX barriers remain the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts China's data centre electricity consumption to quadruple to 774 TWh by 2030, driven by AI workload growth.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets the size of the incremental Chinese power demand pool that generators, grid equipment vendors and IPPs can underwrite capex against.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie forecasts China's data centres

insights.claim: Data centres triple their share of China's total power consumption to 6% by 2030 and scale to 17% by 2060, making compute a structural rather than marginal driver of Chinese electricity demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 17% end-state share means data centre siting decisions become a first-order input to Chinese generation and transmission planning.
insights.quote: Data centre demand share triples to 6% of total power consumption by 2030, scaling to 17% by 2060
insights.locator: Data centre demand share triples to 6%

insights.claim: AI training is driving more energy-intensive infrastructure while the rapid expansion of inference adds a growing base of sustained electricity demand, so the two workload types load the grid differently.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Training reads as lumpy, relocatable peak load; inference reads as sticky always-on baseload near demand centres - different assets serve each.
insights.quote: AI training is driving more energy-intensive infrastructure, while the rapid expansion of inference is adding a growing base of sustained electricity demand
insights.locator: AI growth and policy bring compute and power planning together

insights.claim: Data centre power consumption is expected to keep growing even as China's broader electricity-demand growth moderates, decoupling compute load from the overall demand cycle.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Compute demand becomes the growth engine of Chinese power even in a slowing macro-electricity environment - a defensive demand theme.
insights.quote: these trends are expected to keep data-centre power consumption growing even as China’s broader electricity-demand growth moderates

insights.claim: China's 15th Five-Year Plan calls for coordinated development of computing infrastructure and green electricity, formalising 'compute-power synergy' as national policy rather than an industry preference.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Policy backing de-risks investment in co-located renewable-plus-datacentre projects and signals mandated green procurement.
insights.quote: The 15th Five-Year Plan calls for the coordinated development of computing infrastructure and green electricity.

insights.claim: Recent Chinese energy policies are pushing direct green power supply arrangements and the adoption of more flexible computing loads, turning green sourcing into an operational requirement for operators.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch for growth in direct PPAs and green power trading volumes tied to data centre offtake in China.
insights.quote: recent energy policies are driving direct green power supply and the adoption of more flexible computing loads

insights.claim: Access to reliable, cost-competitive and lower-carbon electricity is becoming a determinant of where and how new data centre capacity is developed, elevating power sourcing above traditional siting criteria.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Power cost and carbon intensity become the screening variable for data centre site selection - favouring regions with cheap firm renewables.
insights.quote: access to reliable, cost-competitive and lower-carbon electricity will play a growing role in determining where and how new data-centre capacity is developed
insights.locator: Data centres are becoming an increasingly important part

insights.claim: The historical model in which data centres cluster around major cities and technology hubs for customers, skilled labour, network infrastructure and low-latency connectivity is being displaced by electricity availability as a siting driver.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A reusable siting model: 'power follows compute' inverting to 'compute follows power' reprices land, grid access and renewable-rich regions.
insights.locator: From “Power Follows Compute” to “Compute Follows Power”

insights.claim: Renewable-rich western China offers abundant land and growing renewable generation, creating opportunities to site AI training, batch processing and data storage workloads closer to electricity sources.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Western Chinese provinces become the marginal beneficiary of AI capex - watch land, grid interconnection and renewable buildout there.
insights.quote: Renewable-rich regions in western China offer abundant land and growing renewable generation capacity
insights.locator: This is accelerating a shift towards a “compute follows power” model

insights.claim: Eastern demand centres will retain latency-sensitive workloads such as AI inference and financial services, producing a division of labour between eastern demand centres and western power-rich computing hubs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Two distinct infrastructure markets emerge: premium low-latency eastern capacity versus commodity power-cheap western capacity.
insights.quote: creating an emerging division of labour between eastern computing demand centres and western power-rich computing hubs
insights.locator: Eastern demand centres are likely to retain

insights.claim: Eight national hubs are expected to remain the dominant centres of China's computing capacity through 2060, commanding over 70% of total data centre capacity even as renewable-rich locations expand gradually.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Concentration means grid, cooling and equipment demand stays clustered - a targetable eight-location infrastructure spend map.
insights.quote: Eight national hubs to command over 70% of total data centre capacity
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie expects eight national hubs

insights.claim: Grid constraints, alongside continued renewable generation growth, are the mechanism expected to push capacity expansion outside the designated national hubs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Grid congestion, not commercial preference, is the forcing function for geographic dispersion of Chinese compute.
insights.quote: grid constraints and continued growth in renewable generation are likely to support gradual expansion in renewable-rich locations outside the designated hubs
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie expects eight national hubs

insights.claim: New power architectures, battery storage and intelligent workload scheduling could convert data centres from passive base loads into demand-side flexibility providers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Creates a new revenue and value stack for operators and a demand-response market opportunity for storage and software vendors.
insights.quote: New power architectures, battery storage and intelligent workload scheduling could transform data centres into demand-side flexibility providers
insights.locator: Data centres become more flexible load resources

insights.claim: Deferrable workloads can be shifted into windows of abundant renewable generation or lower electricity prices, granting computing loads significant temporal elasticity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Temporal elasticity compresses peak power procurement costs and changes how compute capex is valued against power opex.
insights.quote: thereby granting computing loads significant temporal elasticity
insights.locator: For workloads that do not require immediate processing

insights.claim: Data centres can act as strategic demand sinks to absorb curtailed renewables in oversupplied regions as renewable generation expands.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A curtailment-absorption role improves renewable project economics in oversupplied provinces and supports cheap-power data centre siting.
insights.quote: data centres can act as strategic demand sinks to absorb curtailed renewables in oversupplied regions

insights.claim: Data centre carbon emissions in China are forecast to peak by 2035 as renewable power penetration increases, while data centre demand for green electricity rises substantially through 2060.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 2035 emissions peak with rising green demand points to sustained long-dated offtake for Chinese renewables.
insights.quote: Carbon emissions from data centres to peak by 2035 as green power mandates tighten
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie expects data-centre demand for green electricity

insights.claim: The binding constraint on compute-power synergy is commercial and institutional, not physical grid planning: data security and SLA concerns during cross-regional migration, weak operator and tenant willingness to participate, and a heavy initial CAPEX burden.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Bottleneck sits in contracts, security standards and capex financing - watch for policy mechanisms that subsidise upfront cost before betting on rapid westward migration.
insights.quote: stimulate the willingness of operators and tenants to actively participate, and implement targeted mechanisms to alleviate the heavy initial CAPEX burden
insights.locator: The next challenge extends far beyond physical grid planning

insights.claim: The direction of travel is that computing is beginning to follow power, but commercial, security and institutional architectures must evolve before the shift is commercially viable.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frames the timing risk: the physical thesis is right but monetisation lags until institutional plumbing catches up.
insights.quote: The direction of travel is clear: computing is beginning to follow power, but our commercial, security, and institutional architectures must urgently evolve to make this commercially viable.
